extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students learning proof techniques (epsilon-delta limits and induction)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for constructing rigorous epsilon-delta proofs for limits and for writing correct mathematical induction proofs, including common lemmas, choices for δ/ε, structural conventions, and typical pitfalls to avoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness of limits (epsilon-delta proof)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove the limit of a function at a point is unique: assume lim_{x→a} f(x)=K and lim_{x→a} f(x)=L and show K=L by proving |K−L|<ε for arbitrary ε>0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pick ε>0. Use the convergence hypotheses to find δ_K and δ_L so that |f(x)−K|<ε/2 and |f(x)−L|<ε/2 when 0<|x−a|<δ_K/δ_L. Let δ = min{δ_K, δ_L} and apply the triangle inequality: |K−L| ≤ |f(x)−K| + |f(x)−L| < ε. (Typical pattern: split ε into ε/2 parts and take minimum of δ's.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Linearity of limits — scalar multiplication
rubrics_metrics.description: If lim_{x→a} f(x)=K then lim_{x→a} c·f(x)=c·K for scalar c ∈ R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given ε>0 choose δ so that |f(x)−K| < ε/(|c|+1) when 0<|x−a|<δ; this avoids division-by-zero problems when c=0. Then |c f(x) − c K| ≤ |c|·|f(x)−K| < |c|·ε/(|c|+1) < ε. (Pattern: choose ε divided by a constant that safely handles c=0 by adding +1.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Linearity of limits — sum of functions
rubrics_metrics.description: If lim_{x→a} f(x)=K and lim_{x→a} g(x)=L then lim_{x→a} (f(x)+g(x)) = K+L.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given ε>0, pick δ_K, δ_L so that |f(x)−K|<ε/2 and |g(x)−L|<ε/2 when 0<|x−a|< respective δ's. Let δ = min{δ_K,δ_L} and use triangle inequality: |(f+g)−(K+L)| ≤ |f−K| + |g−L| < ε. (Pattern: split ε evenly; take min of δ's.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Product of limits — rewriting and bounding
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove lim_{x→a} f(x)g(x) = K L, rewrite |f g − K L| = |f(g−L) + L(f−K)| and bound the two resulting terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You must control |f(x)| near a. Use a lemma (e.g., Lemma 6.5.9) to obtain bounds of the form |K|/2 ≤ |f(x)| ≤ 3|K|/2 for x close to a. Then choose δs so that |g−L| and |f−K| are small in proportion to ε with denominators depending on |K| and |L| (text uses denominators 3|K|+1 and 2|L|+1 to avoid problems when K or L = 0). Let δ = min of these δs and apply the triangle inequality to get total < ε.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of bounding lemma near limit point (Lemma 6.5.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f(x) → K as x→a, then there exists δ>0 such that when 0<|x−a|<δ we have |K|/2 ≤ |f(x)| ≤ 3|K|/2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This technical lemma provides a uniform bound on |f(x)| in a punctured neighborhood of a, which is crucial when dividing by f(x) or when |f(x)| multiplies another small quantity. Use this to avoid dividing by arbitrarily small numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal limit (limits of 1/g)
rubrics_metrics.description: If lim_{x→a} g(x) = L and L ≠ 0, then lim_{x→a} 1/g(x) = 1/L.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure g(x) is bounded away from 0 near a (apply Lemma 6.5.9 to get |g(x)| > |L|/2). Choose δ to make |g(x)−L| small enough so that |1/g − 1/L| = |L−g|/(|L||g|) < ε. Combine δs and use the bound on |g(x)| to control the denominator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ratio of limits via reciprocal and product
rubrics_metrics.description: If lim f = K and lim g = L ≠ 0, then lim (f/g) = K/L by writing f/g = f·(1/g) and applying product & reciprocal results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First prove limit of reciprocal 1/g, then apply product-of-limits theorem. Ensure prerequisites (L ≠ 0 and bounds) are verified.

rubrics_metrics.name: General epsilon-delta proof patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical strategies for epsilon-delta proofs include splitting ε into parts (e.g., ε/2), taking δ = min{δ_i} from multiple constraints, and avoiding divisions by zero by adjusting denominators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common anti-patterns: forgetting to take min of δ's, failing to control multiplicative terms like |f(x)|, or dividing by constants that might be zero. Use explicit choices (ε/(|c|+1), ε/(3|K|+1), etc.) to avoid edge cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose δ as minimum of required δs
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple convergence conditions are needed, pick δ = min{δ_1, δ_2, ...} so all conditions hold simultaneously in 0<|x−a|<δ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is repeatedly used across proofs (uniqueness, sum, product, reciprocal). Make the choice explicit in the write-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dividing by zero when choosing epsilon fractions
rubrics_metrics.description: When forming fractions of ε for intermediate bounds, add +1 (or otherwise ensure denominator is nonzero) to expressions like |c|, 3|K|, 2|L| to avoid problems when those constants are zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in text: ε/(|c|+1), ε/(3|K|+1), ε/(2|L|+1). This trick prevents undefined expressions and handles edge cases cleanly.

rubrics_metrics.name: State and label proof structure explicitly (induction)
rubrics_metrics.description: When using induction, clearly indicate that induction is being used and label the base case and the inductive step in the write-up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the proof structure obvious so a reader (or marker) can quickly check base case and inductive implication. Include a concluding line like 'By mathematical induction the result holds for all n.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction base case requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove the base case P(1) (or P(ℓ) for generalized induction) explicitly; induction requires a valid base case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to check the base case (or checking the wrong base) can make the entire induction invalid (see examples: false 'n+1 < n' statement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductive step requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove the implication P(k) ⇒ P(k+1) for all relevant k, using the inductive hypothesis explicitly to derive the next case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the inductive hypothesis, manipulate it to obtain P(k+1), and ensure any algebraic operations preserve inequalities (check signs when multiplying).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of well-ordering / minimal counterexample as induction justification
rubrics_metrics.description: An induction proof can be justified by considering the set of counterexamples B and using the well-ordering principle to derive a contradiction from the minimal element of B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a standard proof-sketch: define G and B, assume B nonempty, take minimal ℓ∈B, derive contradiction from P(ℓ−1) ⇒ P(ℓ). Note this argument hides a proof-by-contradiction step; be explicit if using it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make sure all hypotheses are used and highlighted
rubrics_metrics.description: During a proof, verify that every stated hypothesis (e.g., x > −1) is actually used; point out how and where it is applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the (1+x)^n inequality proof the hypothesis x > −1 is necessary to ensure 1+x>0 when multiplying both sides of an inequality. If a hypothesis is unused, the proof likely has a gap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check domain and small-index edge cases in induction
rubrics_metrics.description: When performing induction starting at ℓ>1 or using arguments that assume k≥2, ensure the inductive step holds for the first k in the domain; do not tacitly assume availability of an extra element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pólya's horses example: the inductive overlap argument fails at k=1; explicitly verify the inductive step for the smallest k in the domain and account for any special cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction is not the same as algebraic termwise summation
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't confuse the inductive step with mere termwise addition; the inductive step must be a logical implication P(k) ⇒ P(k+1), and showing equality by adding terms is a valid technique only if placed within that implication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state the inductive hypothesis and show how adding (k+1) to both sides (or analogous manipulation) yields P(k+1). Avoid circular or handwavy reasoning that skips the logical structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Display and comment on subtle steps for the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: When a proof step uses a subtle fact (e.g., sign of a multiplier, or well-ordering), make that explicit to help the reader follow and to prevent mistakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should point out where assumptions are used (e.g., 'since x>−1 we have 1+x>0 so the inequality sign does not flip'). This improves clarity and robustness of the proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicitly handle special numeric cases in inequalities
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving inequalities by induction for n≥ℓ, choose the correct base value and use that lower bound in the inductive step (e.g., proofs that use k≥5 exploit k≥5 to obtain k^2 ≥ 5k).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the domain of n at the outset and ensure any numeric inequalities in the inductive step legitimately use that domain bound; show how it implies the required relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present counterexamples / misproofs as instructive anti-patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: False 'proofs' and misproofs (e.g., polynomial primes, 'n+1<n', Pólya's horses) should be analyzed to reveal the exact logical flaw (missing base case, vacuous implication, tacit assumption).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When critiquing or learning from misproofs, identify whether the problem is a missing base case, an inductive step that never applies, or an assumption invalid for the minimal index. Use such examples to illustrate common pitfalls.
